newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Profiles of Indonesian parties contesting May poll.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of Indonesian parties contesting May poll.

text.p: Following are profiles of the three political parties legally permitted to contest Indonesia's May 29 general elections for the 425 elected seats in the 500-seat House of Representatives.
The remaining 75 seats are alloted to the military which does not vote. The election campaign runs from April 27 to May 23.

GOLKAR - Founded in 1964 by a group of soldiers and civilians to offset the influence of the Communist Party of Indonesia, which was subsequently banned after being blamed for an abortive coup bid in 1965 which led to then general Suharto replacing founding President Sukarno as head of state.

Golkar, which stands for "functional groups", has been the dominant party during President Suharto's 30-year rule. It claims a membership of 36 million out of the country's 200 million population. Its general chairman is Information Minister Harmoko, the first civilian to hold the position.

Golkar officials say they have set a target of 70.02 percent of the 124.7 million voters in the coming election compared with 68 percent of the poll in 1992 and 73 percent in 1987. It is the richest party backed by the military, government bureaucracy and leading businessmen.

In its manifesto, Golkar is pushing government programmes ranging from infrastructural, industrial and agricultural development to social welfare through the sprawling archipelago of more than 17,000 islands.

UNITED DEVELOPMENT PARTY (PPP) - A Moslem-oriented party, it arose from the merger under government pressure of four Islamic parties in 1973. The PPP is mainly rural-based, with much of its support on the main island of Java.
Officials say they do not have a membership figure.
The PPP is chaired by veteran politician Ismail Hasan Metareum, who said the party's campaign theme would be "justice".
The PPP won 17 percent of the vote and 62 seats in parliament in 1992 compared with a peak of 99 seats in 1977.
INDONESIAN DEMOCRATIC PARTY (PDI) - The Christian-Nationalist PDI was also formed under government pressure from several Christian and nationalist parties at the same time as the PPP in 1973.

It has been riven by factional strife since its leader elected for a five-year term in 1993, Megawati Sukarnoputri, was ousted by government-backed rebels headed by deputy parliamentary speaker Surjadi in June last year. Megawati, daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno, has been fighting her ouster through the courts.
Electoral authorities have refused to accept her candidates' list for the forthcoming election and she has told her supporters not to take part in the campaign.
The PDI, which won 15 percent of the vote in 1992, claims a membership of 16 million. Surjadi said its aim was to promote democracy, social justice and the spirit of nationalism.
